name: mercury
why: A logic and functional language with declarative determinism rules, an uncommon paradigm worth an afternoon.

brief.what_it_is: Mercury is a logic/functional programming language, described on its homepage as combining the clarity and expressiveness of declarative programming with advanced static analysis and error detection. Programs are written in Mercury source code and compiled by the Mercury toolchain. The homepage says the execution algorithm is highly optimized and claims efficiency far beyond existing logic programming systems and close to conventional systems. The package metadata lists tools such as mmc, mmake, mdb and mdprof, but I did not see these in the pages I read, so treat that list as unverified.
brief.why_it_exists: The project aims at large-scale program development, with the homepage citing modularity, separate compilation, and optimization/time trade-offs, and the about text calling it "a general purpose language intended to support the creation of large, reliable and efficient applications."
brief.how_it_works: The homepage and README do not explain the mechanism in detail. They say the compiler is itself written in Mercury, so it must be bootstrapped from an existing source distribution. The README also mentions two backends, C (low-level, GCC or Clang) and high-level targets C#, Java, and C.
brief.install_notes: Not Homebrew-specific. Source downloads are on the downloads page, and Debian packages are also available. Building from git requires an existing Mercury install to bootstrap, ideally using a release-of-the-day source that roughly matches the age of the git revision; README.bootstrap covers this. Platform-specific READMEs exist for Linux, macOS, FreeBSD, OpenBSD, AIX, HP-UX, Solaris, Windows (Visual C, MSYS2, Cygwin), and Docker. I did not read any of them.
brief.standout: Mercury is a rare logic/functional language that is compiled, has static analysis and error detection, and is designed for large programs rather than being purely academic. The scout note mentions declarative determinism rules, but neither the homepage nor the GitHub README I read describes determinism explicitly, so I could not confirm that claim from these sources.
brief.status: Maintained, with evidence from the homepage. The news list shows Mercury 22.01.9 released with the date 30 August 2026, and a color diagnostics feature dated 24 June 2024. The copyright runs to 2013–2026. The 2026 date looks unusual next to the 2023–2024 items, so the writer should check it before relying on it. I did not see a commit history or release page.
brief.caveats: Compiler is GPL and the libraries and runtime are LGPL with a static-linking exception. Bootstrapping is required to build from git. The GitHub README points to a LIMITATIONS.md file listing ways the implementation falls short of its goals; I did not read it. The homepage's documentation link returned a 404 when I fetched it. The Homebrew caveats field is empty.

judge.reason: Mercury’s logic-functional model and explicit mode and determinism checking make declarative programming practical for efficient, large-scale software—a distinctive language worth exploring.

entry.title: Mercury
entry.tldr: A compiled logic/functional language built for large programs, with static analysis that catches errors before anything runs.
entry.deeper_look:
Mercury is a declarative programming language that mixes logic and functional programming. Its homepage describes it as combining "the clarity and expressiveness of declarative programming with advanced static analysis and error detection features." Programs are compiled by the Mercury toolchain, and the homepage claims the execution is highly optimized, far faster than older logic programming systems and close to conventional ones.

The project's stated aim is scale. The about text calls it "a general purpose language intended to support the creation of large, reliable and efficient applications," and the homepage points to modularity, separate compilation, and optimization trade-offs. That is a different goal from most logic languages, which tend to live in research or small scripts.

The compiler is written in Mercury itself, so building it from git requires an existing Mercury install. There are two kinds of backend: a low-level one that goes through C with GCC or Clang, and high-level ones targeting C#, Java, and C. The long list of executables Homebrew installs (mmc, mmake, mdb, mdprof and others) suggests a full toolchain with a debugger and profilers, though the brief did not confirm what each does.

The door here is a paradigm: describing what is true about a problem and letting the compiler check your description, instead of spelling out steps. If you have only seen Prolog in passing, a compiled and statically analysed relative is a different experience.
entry.install:
brew install mercury
# Homebrew lists openjdk as a dependency. Source and Debian packages are on the download page.
